source.title: Learning Optimal Representations with the Decodable Information Bottleneck
source.authors: Yann Dubois; Douwe Kiela; D. Schwab; Ramakrishna Vedantam

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some plots are represented only by figure descriptions, but the extracted sharpness results are reported numerically in tables.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures the association between magnitude-aware sharpness and train–test generalization gaps across trained CNNs, then compares that association with other measures and across additional settings.
record.gate_note: Appendix E.1 uses arbitrary-label fitting to compare predictive-family complexity, but does not report held-out performance for that test, so it does not test V1. Rows below cover the study’s reported sharpness correlations; table comparisons to other measures are not separately extracted.
record.test_reason: The study measures magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps using a modified perturbation criterion (V7). It also directly compares dropout with no regularization on held-out performance (V6), which the record overlooks.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors propose DIB to learn representations that support downstream generalization, find V-minimality predictive of generalization, and report that their sharpness implementation predicts poorly across heterogeneous datasets and architectures. Their ordinary-classification experiments also find dropout competitive with DIB on MNIST and better on CIFAR10+MNIST.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows Jiang et al. (2020) in sweeping trained CNN hyperparameters and correlating a measure with the generalization gap. Its sharpness implementation measures log-likelihood differences, and it varies representation size instead of optimizer and weight decay in the main experiment; additional experiments sweep datasets, architectures and individual hyperparameters.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sharpness correlation varies with the gap metric and swept hyperparameter: Table 2 reports different accuracy and log-loss correlations; Table 4 reports different values for weight decay, representation size, VIB β, learning rate and dropout.

fits_no_version.finding: V-minimality predicts generalization and DIB improves downstream performance in several experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation decodability of arbitrary within-class labels can predict generalization, and suppressing it can improve downstream performance.

record.problems: The sharpness implementation differs from Jiang et al.’s implementation, including measuring log-likelihood differences. The main comparison uses models on CIFAR10; additional heterogeneous results are average correlations across settings and include near-zero or negative sharpness correlations. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the correlations.
record.rows_left_out: No other sharpness rows omitted. Table 2 comparison values for V-minimality and other baselines, and Table 4 values for the paper’s V-minimality probe, are not sharpness results and are not included.

untested.parts: No matched natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy comparison; Appendix E.1 reports random-label training fit only.
No held-out error sweep beyond the width required for interpolation. The width experiments assess training fit or representation decodability.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected held-out performance comparison or isolation of local connectivity.
Batch size varies in the model collection, but no small-versus-large-batch held-out performance comparison under a fixed epoch budget is reported.
No direct test of very small training sets, excessive dropout causing underfitting, or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.

No exact replication of the original accuracy-based perturbation criterion, full norm-and-margin comparison, or separate within-family SVHN correlation. The heterogeneous results do not isolate convolutional networks.
No removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

missing.what: Dropout versus no-regularization test accuracy: MNIST 98.68 ± 0.04% versus 98.29 ± 0.05%; CIFAR10+MNIST 48.86 ± 0.17% versus 46.49 ± 0.07%. These direct V6 results are neither recorded nor declared omitted.

Ordinary downstream ERM test log loss with dropout 1.49 ± 0.00, no regularization 4.62 ± 0.00, and stochastic representations 4.34 ± 0.04. Record the two-stage setup and that dropout remains active during downstream training. The worst-ERM results deliberately maximize test loss and should be distinguished from ordinary training.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Table 1 Avg. row; Appendix D.1.2

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V6 or V7. Table 2's 0.484 is a cited original-source result and must not supply this study's verdict. Sharpness uses relative weight perturbations with a log-likelihood-change criterion rather than the original accuracy-change criterion. Negative Table 4 values describe numerical direction; no uncertainty establishes significant reversal.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out accuracy comparison for naturally labeled versus randomly labeled data.
No test-error sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison as the claim version defines it.
No test of dropout’s effect as the claim version defines it.

The study measures correlations for its sharpness magnitude implementation, but does not test weight perturbations across the original convolutional family on both CIFAR-10 and SVHN without augmentation as specified in the version.
No removal and retraining of memorized examples.
